explanation: Failure to sustain primary frequency response can lead to instability during disturbances.
Lack of frequency responsiveness in gas turbines can impair grid stability during disturbances.

source: Article 9.6.2.1 of the pro forma LGIA
explanation: Speed governors must be in automatic mode to ensure proper primary frequency response.
The maximum steady-state operating limit of a generator may be less than its nameplate capacity, affecting primary frequency response calculations.
Droop curves must be implemented without steps to ensure linear frequency response proportional to error.

source: pro forma LGIA Section 9.6.4.2 and pro forma SGIA Section 1.8.4.2
explanation: Generating facilities must provide sustained primary frequency response until system frequency returns to within the deadband parameter during abnormal and sustained frequency deviations.
Electric storage resources not providing online service cannot be required to provide primary frequency response.
Resources with artificial minimum set points can be managed case-by-case if sufficient primary frequency response is available.
Wind generating facilities must comply with a maximum 5 percent droop parameter for primary frequency response.
The deadband must not exceed ±0.036 Hz to prevent unnecessary governor adjustments during minor frequency deviations.
The governor must adjust real power output within 2 seconds for frequencies outside the 59-61 Hz range to maintain stability.
Excessive droop may reduce the ability to maintain frequency during disturbances.
Transition between charging and discharging is only required if necessitated by droop/deadband settings and technically feasible.
Excessive droop parameters may cause instability in frequency regulation when connected to the transmission system.
Governor deadband and droop parameters must be within specified limits to ensure proper frequency response.
Enforces governor parameter limits to ensure frequency response compliance with NERC standards.
